messages.content: What is the largest planet in the universe?

function.name: space_star_info
function.description: Retrieve information about a particular star in the universe. Note that the provided function is in Python 3 syntax.

information.description: The type of information needed about the star.

message.content:
There isn’t one “universal” biggest planet—planetary sizes keep being pushed out further as astronomers discover more worlds—and even within our own Solar System the definition of what counts as a *planet* versus a *brown dwarf* gets fuzzy when you get above roughly 13 Jovian masses. **In practice** | Category | Typical Size / Mass | |----------|---------------------| | **Largest planets in the Solar System** | Gas‑giant Saturn – ≈ 9.5 R⊕ (≈ 0.84 RJ). Ice‑guy Neptune – ≈ 3.88 R⊕ (≈ 0.36 RJ). | | **Exoplanets exceeding Jupiter’s size** | Many hot Jupiters reach 1–2× Jupiter’s radius. For example,
• **WASP‑17b** has a radius ≃ 1.99 RJ.
• **HD 209458b** (the first transiting exoplanet detected) has ≃ 1.38 RJ.
• Some sub‑stellar objects called “super‑Jupiters” approach 2–3 RJ before their interiors become compressed enough that additional mass does not increase radius much. | | **Massive planetary candidates** | Objects near the deuterium‑fusion threshold (~13 MJ) sit right between massive planets and low‑mass brown dwarfs. Examples include **HR 8799 c/d/e**, each ∼ 5–10 MJ, orbiting a young A‑type star. | Because detection methods favor close‑in, inflated planets (hot Jupiters), many of the very large ones we know come from transit surveys rather than direct imaging. As instrumentation improves—especially high‑contrast imagers on next‑generation telescopes—we’ll find more extreme cases, perhaps pushing the upper envelope higher. So while we don’t yet have a single object that claims the title of “largest planet ever found,” the current record holders among confirmed exoplanets hover just under twice Jupiter’s radius, and anything significantly bigger would likely cross into the realm of brown dwarfs.
message.reasoning:
The user asks: "What is the largest planet in the universe?" We need to answer based on known data. Largest planets discovered so far include HD 100546 b (a protoplanet) and possibly others like WASP-17b etc. But we can mention that currently the largest confirmed exoplanets have radii around ~2 Jupiter radii; e.g., HAT-P-32b (~1.8 R_J), or some super-Jupiters up to ~2.5 R_J.

But also there might be gas giants with masses >10 M_jupiter but radius not huge due to compression. So maybe the question expects an explanation that no single definitive largest planet exists because new discoveries happen constantly. Provide context: In our solar system, Neptune is largest ice giant, Saturn is largest gas giant. Exoplanets larger than Jupiter exist, such as Kepler-7b, etc. Also mention that there's theoretical limit at ~13 Jupiter masses beyond which deuterium fusion occurs making it brown dwarf.

We should respond accordingly. No tool call required.
